title: Indonesia - East Kalimantan Project for Emission Reductions Results Project : Inspection Panel Report and Recommendation on a Request for Inspection
text:
Report No. 198070-ID



 The Inspection Panel

 Report and Recommendation
 on a
 Request for Inspection

 INDONESIA:
East Kalimantan Project for
 Emission Reductions Results
 (P166244)




 March 17, 2026
  The Inspection Panel Report and Recommendation
 on a
 Request for Inspection

 Indonesia: East Kalimantan Project for Emission Reductions Results (P166244)


A. Introduction

1. On November 3, 2025, the Inspection Panel (the “Panel”) received a Request for
Inspection (the “Request”) related to the World Bank (the “Bank”) financed Indonesia: East
Kalimantan Project for Emission Reductions Results (P166244) (the “Project” or the “ER
Program”). The Request was submitted by a local, non-governmental organization (NGO) –
Perkumpulan Nurani Perempuan (PNP) – representing members of the Long Isun community
in East Kalimantan. The Requesters have chosen two international NGOs – Accountability
Counsel and the Forest Peoples Programme organization – to advise them in the Panel process.
The Requesters have asked the Panel that their names remain confidential for fear of retaliation.

2. The Request alleges that the Project, designed to incentivize “reduced deforestation
and forest degradation in East Kalimantan, through payments for verified emission reductions
and the distribution of these payments under an agreed Benefit Sharing Plan,” is causing
environmental and social harm to communities. It claims the Project proceeded despite
knowing structural issues – such as delays in recognizing the Long Isun community as
Indigenous Peoples – would be deepened by the Project, and that the Project is exacerbating
unresolved land and boundary disputes and risks of exclusion and infringement on the Long
Isun’s land and land-use rights, as well as worsening social divisions.

3. The Request states that the Project fails to acknowledge the community’s land rights
and customary land use, restricts their ability to maintain cultural practices such as forest rituals
and rotational swidden farming, and creates livelihood losses. It claims the Project “replaces
Indigenous-led forest governance with a market-based, commercial-actor-driven model” that
commodifies forests as carbon assets, marginalizing Indigenous stewardship “under the guise
of sustainable management.” The Request also claims the Benefit Sharing Plan (BSP)
“entrenches structural discrimination” by denying the community direct access to benefits. It
further alleges that Project consultations were inadequate and misrepresented the community’s
Free Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), which has prompted the community to opt-out of the
Project with the expectation that its forest area should be excluded from the ER accounting
area. The Request claims the Project made minimal efforts to ensure women participate in ways
that reflect their needs and cultural roles. The Request alleges the Project has disproportionately
harmed Indigenous women, while failing to recognize, assess, or mitigate these impacts
through inclusive and gender-sensitive consultations. It also alleges that, since raising
concerns, the community has faced “veiled threats.”

4. The Panel registered the Request on December 23, 2025, and Management submitted
its response (the “Management Response” or the “Response”) to the Request on February 11,
2026. A Panel Team (the “Team”) visited Indonesia February 16–27, 2026, to inform its report
and recommendation to the Board of Executive Directors (the “Board”) as to whether an
investigation into the matters alleged in the Request is warranted.



 1
 5. The Panel notes that the Request for Inspection meets all the technical eligibility criteria
set forth in the Panel Resolution. However, the Panel does not recommend an investigation as
it is satisfied that Management has dealt appropriately with those allegations of harm that are
plausibly linked to the Project – including the allegations of institutionalized discrimination
and exclusion caused by implementation of the BSP, inadequate consultations, and fear of
retaliation against the community for its decision not to engage with the Project – and that these
allegations have been or are being addressed. The Panel further notes that the Requesters’ other
allegation – the delays in the MHA recognition process, the disregard of the customary right to
occupy, use, and manage ancestral lands, and the allegation of gender-based violence,
exclusion, and discrimination against women – are not be plausibly linked to the Project.

B. Description of the Project

6. The Project was approved by the Board on November 11, 2020. 1 The Project comprises
results-based payments from the Bank-managed Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF)
Carbon Fund for verified emission reductions in East Kalimantan based on Emissions
Reductions Payment Agreements (ERPAs) signed between the Bank and the Government of
Indonesia (“GoI”). 2 Based on the offered emissions reduction volume, the Project agreed to
finance up to US$110 million, with payments to be made in two tranches, 3 comprising an
Advance Payment and a Final Payment. 4 The Recipient is the Republic of Indonesia, and the
national-level implementing agency is the Ministry of Environment and Forestry (MoEF).5
Following approval of the Project, two ERPAs between the Bank and MoEF were signed on
November 25, 2020. 6 The Project closed on December 31, 2025.

7. The Project Development Objective is to incentivize reduced deforestation and forest
degradation in the Province of East Kalimantan through payment of verified emission
reductions, and to ensure that paid amounts are distributed according to an agreed BSP. 7

8. According to the Project Appraisal Document (PAD), GoI requested financing support
from the FCPF Carbon Fund and submitted an initial proposal in 2016. 8 It identified the
Province of East Kalimantan as a pilot for the FCPF Carbon Fund ER Program, 9 which pays
for the Emissions Reduction (ER) results generated by GoI’s East Kalimantan-Jurisdictional
Emission Reductions Program (EK-JERP). 10 The PAD adds that the Project has provided a
framework for ensuring that EK-JERP’s activities comply with World Bank Operational
Policies related to environmental and social safeguards, benefits are distributed to relevant
stakeholders, and investments are sustained beyond the lifetime of the Bank-funded Project. 11
The PAD also mentions that the ER Program “supports approaches that are pro-poor,

Forestry and the Ministry of Environment. The responsibilities for the ERPAs were split between the Ministry of Forestry,
which is the technical lead on forest governance, management, and REDD+, and the Ministry of Environment, which is
responsible for carbon transactions and results-based payments under the ERPAs. The Provincial Secretary of East Kalimantan
and Sub-National Technical Unit Organizations are responsible for EK-JERP implementation at, respectively, the provincial
and the district level.

 2
 including engagement of local people in forest and land management, livelihood development,
and equitable benefit sharing approaches.” 12

9. The PAD explains the Project comprises the results-based ERPA payments for the
verified ERs generated in East Kalimantan, and that it has no components as investment
operations. 13 As such, this jurisdictional Project is organized as a process that includes two
consecutive steps:

 Step A: Verification of payments for measured and reported ERs. The basis for payments
 under the ERPAs is verified ERs reported by MoEF, whereby the approach to measuring
 emissions in East Kalimantan is consistent with how baseline emissions were estimated
 and assessed by an independent Technical Advisory Panel against the requirements
 stipulated in the FCPF Carbon Fund Methodological Framework. The verified ERs are
 transferred to the FCPF Carbon Fund through a carbon registry system managed by the
 World Bank, acting as Trustee of the Fund, and the ERs paid for are transferred back to
 Indonesia so they can be counted toward the country’s Nationally Determined Contribution
 (NDC). 14

 Step B: Distribution of the ER payments according to the BSP. The proceeds from the
 verified ER payments are shared according to an agreed BSP, designed based on the criteria
 in the FCPF Carbon Fund Methodological Framework and in a manner acceptable to the
 World Bank. The Benefit Sharing Plan (BSP) describes the benefit-sharing arrangements,
 including the distribution mechanism, the flow of funds, and allocation rules for ERPA
 payments and sharing of benefits to agreed beneficiaries. Payments are received by the
 Indonesia Environmental Fund and then transferred to eligible beneficiaries in the form of
 three types of allocations: Responsibility, Performance, and Reward Allocations. 15 Among
 the eligible beneficiaries are Adat communities (i.e., customary communities). 16

10. According to the PAD, the overall Project risk rating was “high.” 17 The Project
triggered the following safeguard policies: Natural Habitats OP/BP 4.04, Forests OP/BP 4.36,
Pest Management OP 4.09, Physical Cultural Resources OP/BP 4.11, Indigenous Peoples
OP/BP 4.10, and Involuntary Resettlement OP/BP 4.12. 18 The PAD states that, as Trustee of
the FCPF Carbon Fund, the Bank reserves the right to initiate separate monitoring of the
implementation of the safeguard plans and the Benefit Sharing Plan annually after the ERPA
date. 19 According to the December 8, 2025, Implementation Status and Results Report, the
overall Project risk rating remains “high” while the safeguards’ rating improved from
“moderately unsatisfactory” to “moderately satisfactory.” 20 Also applicable to the Bank is the

NDC to reduce its GHG emissions by 41 percent by 2030 with international assistance (or 29 percent using its own resources),
relative to a business-as-usual (BAU) scenario. To achieve this target, GoI would need to reduce emissions by 1.1 billion tonnes
of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO₂e), with about 60 percent of the reduction expected to come from the forestry sector. This
would require reducing average annual deforestation from 920,000 ha to 450,000 ha between 2013 and 2020, and further
lowering it to 325,000 ha annually from 2021 to 2030, while also rehabilitating two million ha of degraded peat areas and an
additional 12 million ha of other degraded land.

 Directive on Managing Environmental and Social risks and Impacts for the Emission
Reductions Program under the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility and the BioCarbon Fund
Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes, which became effective on December 24, 2024.
The Directive applies to operations under implementation that were approved prior to this
date. 21

C. Summary of the Request

11. This section summarizes the issues raised in the Request (the full Request is attached
to this Report as Annex I). It alleges the Project is causing significant environmental and social
harm to the Long Isun community. This harm includes exacerbating unresolved land and
boundary disputes, delays in the recognition of the community’s status as Indigenous People –
resulting in potential livelihood losses and the risk of discrimination against it – and exclusion
from benefit-sharing. The Requesters’ claims and allegations are summarized below.

12. Alleged delayed recognition of the Long Isun as Indigenous People. The Request
states that the Long Isun community, which depends on forest and river ecosystems for
subsistence, livelihoods, and cultural survival, has not received formal recognition
(Masyarakat Hukum Adat, MHA) from the Government of Indonesia. It adds that the Long Isun
community identifies as “Masyarakat Adat (Indigenous Peoples) under Indonesian law” and
satisfies the requirements for Indigenous Peoples under the Bank’s safeguard policy, OP/BP
4.10. It states that, in substance, an assessment should have considered the Long Isun
community’s unresolved land boundary conflict and its role in delaying MHA recognition. The
Request alleges the Project exacerbated social conflict and increased risks for the Long Isun
community by including an area subject to an unresolved boundary dispute with a neighboring
community. The Request also claims that a timber concessionaire reached a concession
agreement with another community that covers areas, considered part of Long Isun territory.

13. The Request alleges the Project infringes on the community’s identity and land rights
in different ways, claiming:

 a) Disregard of the customary right to occupy, use, and manage ancestral lands.
 According to the Request, the Project undermines the customary rights of the Long Isun
 community over their ancestral lands – “rights that are the foundation of our identity and
 survival” and are essential to their cultural and spiritual survival. It adds that the Project
 infringes on their ability to maintain cultural practices tied to the land, including forest
 rituals and rotational farming, in breach of the Bank’s Physical Cultural Resources Policy,
 OP/BP 4.11. The Request claims the Project proceeded without securing land tenure,
 respecting Indigenous Peoples stewardship, or providing their community with alternatives
 to sustain their culture and livelihoods. The Request considers banners prohibiting swidden
 agriculture reflect a broader trend in national and regional policy frameworks, adding that
 no distinction is made for customary, small-scale, and ecologically sustainable practices.

 b) Loss of land-based livelihoods for Indigenous Peoples. The Request states the
 community has traditionally sustained itself through small-scale logging, controlled
 swidden farming, and hunting – practices rooted in ecological knowledge that ensures these
 traditional uses of the forest preserve it for future generations. It adds that while the Project

21 Bank Directive: Managing Environmental and Social Risks and Impacts for the Emission Reductions Programs under the

Forest Carbon Partnership Facility and the BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes, December 24,
2024.
 4
  acknowledged that restricting customary practices such as swidden farming could harm
 communities if no alternatives were provided, it “failed to provide mitigation measures,
 livelihood alternatives, or protection mechanism.”

14. Alleged institutionalized discrimination and exclusion caused by the
implementation of the Project’s Benefit-Sharing Plan. The Request states that the Project’s
BSP institutionalizes discrimination and exclusion. Although under the revised BSP
unrecognized groups like the Long Isun community are nominally eligible for the Reward
Allocation, according to the Request major barriers remain to access this allocation. The
Request explains access to the Reward Allocation depends on Pokja 22 validation by a
government-established body which, according to the Request, has no Indigenous
representation and offers no appeals process, allowing exclusionary decisions. According to
the Request, communities must also submit proposals, facilitated by an intermediary agency or
subcontracted NGOs, to access the Reward Allocation, which add another layer of gatekeeping
and discretionary engagements.

15. The Request states that the BSP’s Performance Allocation is mediated through
provincial and district agencies, and in some cases requires partnerships with concessionaires,
to deliver monetary and non-monetary benefits. According to the Request, this model is
structurally harmful to the Long Isun because it forces communities to partner with
concessionaires, including the timber concessionaire with whom the Long Isun has been having
a longstanding conflict. The Request adds that this model denies Indigenous Peoples the right
to self-determined development and violates the Bank’s Indigenous Peoples policy, OP/BP
4.10. The Request concludes that the Project replaces community-based conservation with a
commercialized forest management model, enabling entities that are historically responsible
for deforestation to claim emission reduction credits while Indigenous communities – whose
customary stewardship preserved the forest for generations – face increased restrictions,
bureaucratic exclusion, and threats of criminalization.

16. Alleged inadequate consultations. The Request states consultations with the Long
Isun during Project planning and implementation were “inadequate, misleading, coercive, and
discriminatory from the outset.” It adds that in one consultation conducted for Mahakam Ulu,
only two Adat representatives were present among 100 participants, and both representatives
made it clear that they had no authority to represent the wider Long Isun community. According
to the Request, the facilitators of said consultation promised to return to carry out proper
socialization process, but this never happened. The Request claims the Bank allowed the
Project to proceed without genuine FPIC, relying on signatures on an attendance sheet as
evidence of consent. According to the Request, this resulted in a “sham” FPIC process. The
Request states that, upon learning this, the Long Isun community formally revoked its consent
for, and opted out of the Project with the expectation that its forest area be excluded from the
Project’s emissions reductions calculations. The Request adds that the unanswered community
questions during these consultations – “[W]hat is carbon? How do they collect the carbon? Do
they use planes?” – demonstrate the Project’s failure to conduct consultations in a meaningful
manner.

17. Alleged gender-based violence, exclusion, and discrimination against women. The
Request explains that, for the women of the Long Isun community the forest is not only a
resource but a sacred foundation of life and culture. The Request claims that Project restrictions

22 In Indonesia, “Pokja” is short for Kelompok Kerja, which translates as “Working Group.” This refers to an officially

established, task-based group with defined roles, authority, and a specific mandate.
 5
 on forest-use have directly undermined women’s livelihoods since they depend on forest
resources for food security, medicinal herbs, plants for craft-making, and other non-timber
products to support household income and which generate small-scale, economic activities. It
alleges that because the Project relies on the Government’s MHA recognition process, which
excludes unrecognized groups, the Indigenous women of the Long Isun community are doubly
marginalized. The Request claims Project consultations were neither inclusive nor gender-
sensitive, as women were not given sufficient opportunities to speak or access information in
forms understandable or culturally appropriate to them, and no separate consultations were
held. Lastly, the Request alleges that the Project failed to ensure women in Long Isun had
access to a safe grievance redress mechanism, nor were safeguards put in place to ensure that
women could speak without fear of community backlash or retaliation.

18. Alleged retaliation against the community. The Request states that when community
members raised concerns about the Project, they faced coercion and retaliation instead of
meaningful engagement. The Request includes other instances of retaliation, which the Panel
was asked to keep confidential.

D. Summary of Management Response

19. This section summarizes Management’s Response to the Request (the full Response is
attached to this Report as Annex II). Management states it has carefully reviewed the concerns
raised by the Long Isun community. It states that concerns – such as ambiguities in safeguard
instruments, including the need to revise the BSP and the Indigenous Peoples Plan (IPP) –
raised in the Request have been addressed. However, other concerns either predate or are
unrelated to the Project or are not governed by Bank policy and, therefore, cannot be addressed
by the Project or the Bank. 23 Management states that it recognizes that at the heart of the
Requesters’ concerns is the formal recognition of the Long Isun community as an indigenous
(Adat, or customary law) group. 24

20. Management acknowledges some gaps in following up on the timing and sequencing
of the Government’s reporting on the Environment and Social Management System during
2021–2024, delays and shortcomings in the initial consultation process, and barriers in the
Reward Allocation under the original BSP.25 According to Management, these issues were
identified and addressed during Project implementation. Management concludes that the
Requesters’ rights or interests have not been affected by any alleged failure by the Bank to
implement its policies and procedures. 26 The paragraphs below summarize Management’s
specific responses to the allegations raised in the Request.

21. Alleged delayed recognition of the Long Isun Indigenous Peoples. Management
acknowledges the importance of MHA legal recognition for the Long Isun community. It
highlights that such recognition as an Adat group is governed by Indonesian Law known as
“Masyarakat Hukum Adat” (MHA) legal recognition process. According to Management, this
process is outside the remit of the Project. Management states that the community’s application
for legal MHA started in 2018, and delays in the process are not attributable to the Project
which was approved only in November 2020. 27 Management claims that the ER Program set
up a district-level MHA verification committees to facilitate the recognition process and

23 Management Response, p. vii, para. viii.
24 Management Response, p. 16, para 48.
25 Management Response, p. xiii, para xxxi.
26 Management Response, p. 29, para. 105.
27 Management Response, p. 16, para. 48.

 6
 provided resources to the provincial and district Community Empowerment and Village
Government Agency (Dinas Pemberdayaan Masyarakat dan Pemerintahan Desa) to support
the applications of local communities. Management further explains that the Project could not
guarantee legal MHA recognition, and that Project activities were not preconditioned on such
recognition, nor was this a requirement of Bank policy. 28

22. The Management Response states that the MHA process is widely known to be lengthy,
largely because the responsible local government authorities often lack the financial and
administrative capacities and resources needed to carry out the verification. 29 Management
adds that the process was also delayed due to legacy boundary disputes with a neighboring
community and issuance of a district decree which had endorsed overlapping maps. 30

23. Regarding the alleged disregard of customary right to occupy, use, and manage
ancestral lands and loss of livelihood, Management states that the ER Program does not impose
land-use restrictions. Management also states that the ER Program imposes no regulations
preventing forest fires in Long Isun. 31 Management clarifies that in Indonesia, clearing land by
burning forest for permanent land conversion is expressly prohibited by law. However,
Management emphasizes that the law allows traditional use of fire by customary communities
for swidden agriculture practices under specific conditions. Management states that Long
Isun’s customary Adat Council follows and enforces these practices during the planting season.
Management adds that no complaints by the Long Isun community have been filed with the
local forest authorities about such restrictions. 32

24. The Management Response adds that the banners prohibiting swidden agriculture
referred to in the Request date from 2023, and that these types of banners are typically
displayed near forested areas during dry El Niño periods, such as that experienced in
Kalimantan between June and October 2023. They were issued by the District Disaster Risk
Information Services and are unrelated to the ER Program. 33 The Management Response
emphasizes that the ER Program introduced no new prohibitions on swidden farming or
controlled burning. 34

25. Alleged institutionalized discrimination and exclusion caused by the
implementation of the Project’s Benefit-Sharing Plan. According to the Response, the
territorial and administrative situation of Long Isun bears implications for understanding the
Requesters’ claims in relation to the BSP. Management states that “Long Isun” refers to both
1) the Desa (i.e., the village) of Long Isun, as registered in the Indonesia administrative system
and governed by an elected Village Head, and 2) the Dayak Bahau of Long Isun (Masyarakat
Adat – i.e., the customary community) who live in the territory of Long Isun. Management
states it understands the village also comprises the vast majority of the customary Long Isun
community and there are two leaders – the elected Village Head under the official
administrative system, and the Adat leader of the customary community. 35 The Response
explains that under the original 2021 BSP, 36 the village of Long Isun was eligible to receive a
share of the Performance Allocation, irrespective of MHA legal recognition, which has never

 been required for this allocation. However, the Long Isun community was ineligible for the
Reward Allocation because, at that time, this allocation was limited to communities that had
already received legal MHA recognition. 37 It adds that the Performance Allocation is intended
for villages based on the submission of budget plans developed during village-based
participatory planning, while the Reward Allocation is intended directly for Adat or other
community groups.

26. Management states that in August 2024, the Long Isun Adat community chose to opt-
out of the ER Program and declined the share of 378 million Indonesian Rupiah (IDR) from
the Performance Allocation which the village of Long Isun was eligible to receive from the
Advance Payment the Government had received under one of the two signed ERPAs. The
Response states that the customary community did so on the grounds that the funds would be
administered by the village government rather than the community directly. 38 The Response
also states that while Requesters claim these funds were transferred to them against their will,
Management found no evidence of any such transfer. 39

27. Management clarifies that under the revised 2025 BSP 40, the Long Isun can now receive
monetary benefits through both the Performance Allocation and the Reward Allocation.
Management further explains that, at the Bank’s request and based on feedback from the
Requesters, the Government revised the original BSP to remove the exclusion of non-
recognized customary communities from Reward Allocation. Management notes it expects that
“implementation of the revised BSP will address shortcomings identified in the 2021 version,
including enabling fair and equitable access to funds for communities – such as Long Isun (if
they choose to opt-in) and other adat groups that are not legally recognized by the Government
– that did not received grants or transfers under the advanced payment.” 41

28. The Response also states that, while the Request alleges the revised BSP still requires
them to engage in partnership with the private sector, the ER Program contains no requirement
for such partnerships. 42 Specifically, under the revised BSP the Performance Allocation is
channeled through village government and local government agencies, and the Reward
Allocation is channeled via NGOs. Management also stresses that the revision of the BSP
removed all private sector roles in the BSP, and it introduced a stronger role for Adat
representatives and civil society. 43

29. On the specific claim that the Reward Allocation is contingent on Pokja, Management
explains that the purpose of this allocation is to provide a civil-society-led avenue to access
this allocation, including customary Adat communities. Management adds that outreach and
consultation activities to inform potentially eligible groups of the Reward Allocation have been
delegated to subnational intermediary agencies, and this method had been identified as
appropriate based on the consultation process held in July-October 2025. 44 The Response also
states that proposal requirements had been streamlined with community proposal facilitators
trained in participatory planning practices. Management emphasizes that the revised BSP
modifications were adopted explicitly based on the suggestion made in writing by the

 complainants in the April 7, 2025, GRS case. Moreover, Management states that engagement
with Adat community organizations is a BSP requirement. 45

30. Alleged inadequate consultations. Management states that consultations conducted
were consistent with the requirements of OP/BP 4.01 and OP/BP 4.10. The Management
Response describes that engagement was carried out on all levels – national, provincial, district,
and community – with the participation of Indigenous Peoples’ representation throughout the
Project development and implementation. While consultations were widely conducted,
Management admits that community-led consultations in Kutai and Mahakam Ulu District –
where the Requesters reside – were not conducted in 2020 due to COVID-19 conditions, but
representatives of these two districts, including Long Isun, participated in the district-level
consultations in 2019. 46 Management acknowledges that engagement with the Long Isun
community in the early stages of the ER Program did not sufficiently communicate
participation choices, opt-out options, or grievance channels. Management states that they
worked with the Government to strengthen outreach; however, at that point, the Long Isun
community had decided to opt-out, and requested the Government to cease contacting them in
relation to the ER Program. 47

31. Management believes the Project, as per OP/BP 4.10, requires free, prior, and informed
consultation resulting in broad community support, while the Indigenous Peoples Plan
Framework and the IPP refer to a requirement for consent of relevant communities. According
to Management, with the agreement of the community only two ER measures were
implemented in Long Isun: i) the provision of technical assistance by the local government to
support the legal MHA recognition claim, and ii) the establishment of the Community Forest
Fire Prevention Group (Masyarakat Peduli Api, “MPA”). Management states these measures
were voluntary and carried out at the request of the community. 48 Management cites a meeting
held in August 2024 where the MHA recognition process was discussed together with the
presentation on Forest Carbon Partnership Facility. Management admits this had been poorly
communicated to the Long Isun community, which led to the impression of coercing them into
consenting to the ER Program. Management states the attendance sheet was never used as
evidence of consent. 49 Following such meetings, the community was given two weeks to
deliberate and decide whether to participate in the benefit sharing of the ER Program. 50

32. Alleged gender-based violence, exclusion, and discrimination against women.
According to Management, it is not aware of any adverse impacts on women having occurred
as a result of the Project or the implementation of the BSP. 51 The Management Response adds
that risks of excluding women were identified and mitigation measures have been built into the
design of the BSP. Management explains that the Project conducted a gender assessment and
established a Gender Working Group (Pokja Gender mainstreaming) under the Provincial
Development Planning Agency, and that the BSP securing women’s participation at the village
level decision-making processes in line with Village Law No. 6. Management also notes that
gender-sensitive, stakeholder engagement was conducted during the revision of the BSP and
the IPP. 52

 33. Alleged retaliation against the community. Management states that the Bank
promptly and consistently responded to the Long Isun community’s stated fear of reprisals.
According to Management, they stressed the need to protect complainants from any form of
threat, intimidation, or reprisal through a formal letter sent in April and September 2024 to the
Ministry of Environment, the Ministry of Forestry, and the Provincial Government of East
Kalimantan. Management reiterated this concern verbally in a meeting held in June 2024 with
Government authorities. Management notes that the Requesters had acknowledged and
commended the Bank through a letter received in November 2024 for taking proactive steps in
addressing the allegations of intimidation and retaliation. 53 Furthermore, Management
mentions that no additional incidents of reprisals or intimidation were reported during the
Bank’s visit to Long Isun in February 2025. 54

E. Panel’s Eligibility Assessment, Observations, and Review

34. The Panel’s review is based on information presented in the Request, the Management
Response, relevant documentary evidence, and information gathered through conversations
with different stakeholders during the Team’s visit in Indonesia.

35. Panel Member Evelyn Dietsche (Lead Inspector), Senior Policy Advisor Serge Selwan,
Investigations Officer Camila Jorge do Amaral, and Research Analyst Dion Romano visited
Indonesia February 16–27, 2026, to inform the Panel’s eligibility assessment. During its visit
to East Kalimantan, the Team met with district and provincial authorities of Mahakam Ulu in
Samarinda, as well as with the Requesters and their representatives (from both the Long Isun

with officials of the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Forestry, the Ministry of Environment,

stakeholders for taking the time to share their views and perspectives. The Panel extends

43. Alleged delayed recognition of the Long Isun Indigenous Peoples. During the
Panel’s visit to Long Isun, the Requesters emphasized that the Bank should have supported the
formal recognition of their status as an Adat community before proceeding with the Project.
They added that receiving Adat recognition enables them to apply for the recognition of their
forest as an Adat customary forest. They claimed that the Project has made insufficient efforts
to follow up with the authorities on the progress regarding their Adat recognition. They added
that since their last meeting with Bank staff in February 2025, there has been no further update
by the Bank. The Requesters informed the Panel Team that district authorities informed them
in November 2025 that the MHA legal recognition process was in “the last stage of the process”
and “awaiting signature” from the district head. After the eligibility visit, the Requesters
informed the Panel that there are clerical errors in the documentations they received for the
finalization of their MHA recognition.

44. During the Panel’s meetings, provincial and district authorities shared similar views
concerning the MHA recognition process in general and concerning the Long Isun community.
The East Kalimantan provincial authorities stated that MHA recognition is a common goal that
is supported by Component 1 of the Project. They noted that there are 325 communities in the
province living within forest areas and who can apply for MHA status, which requires
validation by district authorities. They acknowledged that delays occurred in the MHA
recognition process and these were caused by a limited understanding of the process, low
capacity, and a lack of established procedures. The provincial authorities added that, currently,
the validation process includes several steps conducted by district authorities and their
responsibility is to provide district authorities with technical support.

45. The Mahakam Ulu district authorities stated that their administration is one of the
youngest and most remote, and that staff training has been necessary for the processing of MHA
recognition applications. They noted that additional factors contributed to delays including the
applicants’ submission of required documents and the rotation and turnover of district staff.
They explained that various requirements must be met before Adat recognition is granted,
including verification of community territorial boundaries, and that boundary disputes
commonly cause delays. They stated that, in the case of the Long Isun, senior district officials
mediated the land dispute with a neighboring community. They stated that they received all the
 13
 required documents from the Long Isun community for MHA recognition by November 6,
2025, and completed their review on November 10, 2025.

46. During its visit, the Panel was informed by authorities that, with the land dispute now
resolved, the recognition process is merely awaiting the signature of the highest district
authority. The Panel was assured this would be forthcoming soon. The Panel understands that,
at the time of the submission of its recommendation, this signature was still pending. The
authorities also noted that the Long Isun community is privileged, as it receives support from
an external NGO, and emphasized that MHA recognition should be granted to all Adat
communities in accordance with the legal process.

47. Provincial authorities told the Panel that prior to the ER Program, only two customary
communities in East Kalimantan had secured MHA recognition; however, between 2018 and
2026, eight additional customary communities received MHA recognition. They added that 50
customary communities in the Mahakam Ulu district are expected to be granted MHA
recognition. They emphasized that the process requires time and prudence to avoid creating or
exacerbating conflicts among communities. Provincial and district authorities recognized that
the MHA recognition process has provided them with institutional learning experience, and
they attributed to the Project many of the improvements in the process.

48. Provincial and district authorities stated that, once the Long Isun community is
recognized as Adat, it can apply for recognition of its forest as an Adat customary forest.
Provincial authorities clarified that the Adat forest verification process is conducted by the
Ministry of Forestry and can only be initiated after MHA recognition has been obtained. They
told the Panel that there are currently six recognized Adat forests in East Kalimantan. Both
provincial and district authorities also emphasized that the community’s and their objectives
regarding the preservation and protection of the forests in Mahakam Ulu District were aligned
and represented a win-win situation.

49. During the Panel’s meeting, Bank staff explained that the Project is a results-based
operation aimed at “rewarding emission reductions.” Staff emphasized that the Project has
contributed to accelerating the recognition process, including that of the Long Isun community,
by strengthening the financial and institutional capacities of the provincial and district
authorities. This is also noted in the Management Response, which stated that legal MHA
recognition supports the objectives of the Project, and hence, Component 1 of the ER Program
was designed to provide policy and institutional support to address pre-existing risks hindering
the recognition process. 61 Bank staff confirmed that Project support to the district authorities
facilitated settling the boundary dispute between Long Isun and a neighboring community,
which had been a key factor delaying the MHA legal verification process.

50. Alleged institutionalized discrimination and exclusion caused by the
implementation of the Project’s Benefit-Sharing Plan. The Long Isun community informed
the Panel that, despite their withdrawal, the Project continues to include their territory in its ER
accounting. They explained that the carbon stored in Long Isun’s forests is still being measured,
reported, and monetized to generate emission reduction payments. The community said they
felt excluded and discriminated against because, as per the original BSP, the Reward Allocation
only benefited communities with Adat status. They also stated that the BSP forced them to
partner with a private sector timber concessionaire to receive the Performance Allocation.
Community leaders told the Panel that the funds offered under the Advance Payment do not
61 Management Response, p. 18, para. 56.
 14
 reflect the value of their forest, which provides them with livelihoods, food security, medicinal
plants, and other essential products, without having to spend money. They emphasized that they
are unwilling to exchange the forest they have preserved and safeguarded for generations for
money and explained that their rejection of the Project is a matter of principle. They expressed
fear that accepting the BSP allocation could lead to coercion into reaching an agreement with
a timber concessionaire, especially given that the community is not yet recognized as Adat.

51. Leaders in the Long Isun community told the Panel that they considered the
Performance Allocation under the original BSP to be unfair, as each participating village was
equally allocated IDR 378 million,62 regardless of whether it protected the forest or, on the
contrary, contributed to deforestation. They believed that communities that have protected their
forests from deforestation and timber harvesting should receive more money because their
forest stores “more carbon”, than those forests that have been exploited. They told the Panel
that they were aware the BSP had been revised and that some 46 village representatives had
been called to a consultation meeting on the revised BSP and IPP in August 2025. They stated
they only saw the revised BSP after the complaint to the GRS and did not understand it because
the document was long, technical and in English. They said they requested a non-technical
summary in their language from the Project’s consultant but never received it. Additionally,
community leaders noted it was not clear to them how and on what the Performance Allocation
funds could be used. While they understood they must formulate and submit proposals, they
did not know what these proposals could entail. They expressed their preference for receiving
funds directly into a village account so they can use them according to community needs. 63

52. During its meeting with the Panel, provincial authorities acknowledged that non-
recognized Adat communities were not considered eligible for the Reward Allocation in the
original BSP and, consequently, communities did not qualify to receive this allocation from the
Advance Payment. The authorities also acknowledged that the approach for the Performance
Allocation in the original BSP awarding participating villages equally was biased against those
who had protected their forests in the past. They considered that both aspects in the original
BSP constituted weaknesses, which they believe have been addressed in the revised BSP.

53. The provincial authorities explained that, per the revised BSP, the three types of benefit
sharing payments – (1) Responsibility Allocation, (2) Performance Allocation and (3) Reward
Allocation – comprise 25 percent, 65 percent, and 10 percent, respectively, of the Final
Payment. They stated that the Responsibility Allocation is designated to cover Project
operational and implementation costs. They added that under the revised BSP, the Reward
Allocation recognizes local community groups supporting sustainable forest management or
having historically preserved and conserved forests, irrespective of their Adat status.

54. Concerning the Performance Allocation, the authorities confirmed to the Panel team
that the revised BSP introduces an updated formula. They stated that the revision was based on
the feedback received from Bank staff and consulted villages, following the earlier, equal
distribution of IDR 378 million to each participating village. They explained that the new
formula for the Performance Allocation now recognizes village-level efforts to reduce
deforestation and forest degradation against historical baselines, as well as village and
community efforts practicing sustainable forest management all along. They explained that the

 revised formula considers differences in district-level forest coverage and – through allocations
that are adjusted based on an index – better awards villages with greater forest coverage and

is provided to and used by village authorities and, thus, is indirectly benefiting communities.

55. The authorities told the Panel that, together, the Performance and Reward Allocations
guarantee that every eligible village in the province and their respective communities gets
direct and indirect funding. They explained that the updated formula strikes a better balance
between incentivizing forest preservation and protection and rewarding those who have been
doing just that all along. Authorities stated that the Long Isun decision to opt-out was
unfortunate; however, the village and the community can still choose to opt into the Project
and would be entitled to receive the Performance and the Reward Allocations. Authorities
stated that this opportunity exists until approximately 2028, when the Final Payment is
expected to have been fully disbursed.

56. The authorities emphasized the value of the forests upstream of the Mahakam River in
reducing downstream flood risks and noted that the current Government has set an ambitious
target of granting Adat recognition and customary titles to several hundred communities across
East Kalimantan whose sustainable forest management provides this ecosystem service. They
also expressed appreciation for the lessons learned from the ER Program regarding the process
of recognizing Adat communities and the importance of these communities’ stewardship of
their forests.

57. During its visit, the Panel had a joint meeting with the Ministry of Environment, the
Ministry of Forestry, and the Ministry of Finance. They stated that the Project has already
addressed most of the Long Isun community’s concerns, including removing the requirement
of Adat recognition for the Reward Allocation, allowing greater flexibility in how the funds
from the Performance and the Reward Allocations may be used, including on education,
expanding participation for local CSOs, as well as simplifying access to these funds. The
ministries noted that these improvements have not only strengthened the Project and its systems
but also supported the achievement of ambitious national goals related to increasing MHA
recognition and the designation of Adat customary forests.

58. Bank staff told the Panel that, although the Project closed on December 31, 2025, the
ERPAs stipulate that the Government would continue to report on the implementation of the
revised BSP every six months. They added that the Project has contributed to institutional
strengthening at the provincial and district levels, as well as the level of the Community
Empowerment and Village Government Agency. The Bank staff acknowledged the original
BSP needed improving, especially because it excluded non-recognized Adat communities.
Bank staff added it has taken the complaints received through GRS seriously, including the
concerns that the original BSP did not reward those who have been managing their forests well.

59. Alleged inadequate consultations. During the Panel’s visit, the community leaders
told the Panel that consultations were not meaningful, inclusive, or culturally appropriate,
leaving them feeling discriminated against. They said large consultation meetings with many
villages had little representation from Adat communities. Community members shared their
view that the Project did not socialize with them Project-related information, and that this
should have happened prior to their complaint to the GRS. They emphasized that the
 16
 community lacks basic knowledge on how the Project operates, the BSP formula, their
participation, how funds can be allocated, potential implications for their access to the forest
and use of ancestral land, and how carbon is measured and collected. Community members
expressed discontent that the Project did not seek the community’s free, prior, and informed
consent (FPIC) “before taking its carbon,” and that the Project did not act like a guest and
“entered [their] house without first knocking [on] the door or asking for permission.”

60. Provincial authorities and Bank staff acknowledged that initial consultations were
insufficient and that communities were inadequately informed about the Project, its procedures,
participation options, the BSP, and the ways through which communities can raise concerns.
Authorities recognized that COVID-19 restrictions and logistical challenges in reaching some
communities caused delays and gaps. Provincial authorities told the Panel that consultations in
2020 were held by phone and later attempts to visit the community were prevented by
dry-season conditions. They told the Panel that outreach and participation were strengthened
following the GRS complaint which the Bank received in March 2024. Between 2024 and
2025, consultations on the BSP regarding allocations from the Advance Payment reached 441
villages and 150 community beneficiaries. In September 2025 additional consultations on the
revisions of the BSP and IPP involved more than 1,000 participants. Bank staff added that the
Bank will continue to support the local government with its socialization of the revised BSP.

61. When asked about further engagement with the Long Isun community on the revised
BSP, provincial authorities and Bank staff stated that once the community chose to opt-out of
the ER Program’s benefit sharing and requested no further contact, this decision was fully
respected by both authorities and Bank staff. The authorities also stated that PNP participated
in the revisions of the BSP and the IPP.

62. Alleged gender-based violence, exclusion, and discrimination against women.
Concerning the allegations of Gender-Based Violence (GBV) raised in the Request, the Panel
notes that GBV is any harmful act based on gender differences, including physical, sexual, or
psychological harm, threats, coercion, or denial of liberty. 64 While engagement with the Long
Isun community may not have been sufficiently gender-sensitive or inclusive, the women the
Panel spoke with did not report any incidents of physical or sexual violence, or other acts
amounting to what would be considered GBV as per the above definition.

63. During its visit, the Panel met with women of the Long Isun community who raised
concerns about “violence,” exclusion, discrimination, and loss of livelihoods. They explained
that banners prohibiting traditional swidden agriculture were placed in the forest without
warning or their consent, creating fear that the Project may restrict their forest access. The
women emphasized that they rely on the forest for medicinal herbs, artisanal weaving, and
food, and that restrictions would disproportionately affect them, as these resources are essential
to their livelihoods, household food security, and the community’s cultural continuity. The
women told the Panel that consultations were not inclusive or gender-sensitive, and that they
were not given opportunities to voice their concerns meaningfully. They claimed there were no
women-specific meetings to provide them with Project information and that they felt “violated”
when Project consultants pressured them to join the PFIC meeting without advance warning
and they were “caught in the kitchen” to sign the attendance sheet.

 64. Bank staff told the Panel that a gender analysis identified cultural and economic barriers
limiting women’s participation in decision-making and planning processes. The Management
Response states that, following the GRS complaint, stakeholder engagement was conducted

65. The Panel recognizes the importance of forest resources and traditional farming to
women’s livelihoods, food security, and cultural roles, as well as the broader challenges faced
by women, particularly Adat women, including discrimination and exclusion. The Panel notes
the alleged restrictions on accessing the forest are unrelated to the Project, and that women
confirmed they continue to farm and access the forest and its resources as usual.

66. Disregard of the customary right to occupy, use, and manage ancestral lands. The
Long Isun community told the Panel during its visit, that it practices swidden farming
(including rotational burning) to restore soil fertility and ensure food security. The community
stated that prohibiting this practice, without providing viable alternatives, directly threatens
household subsistence and increases dependency on external programs. They added that the
Project conflicts with their traditional farming practices and had not sought their FPIC prior to
imposing these restrictions. Community members told the Panel that signage had been put up
in many different locations within the province.

67. During its meeting with the provincial and district authorities, the FMU (Forest
Management Units - Kesatuan Pengelolaan Hutan) stated it has established community-based
fire prevention and suppression groups that patrol communities, especially in the dry season.
The FMU explained that the banners are part of a national campaign following a 2020
presidential decree mandating measures to improve forest and land fire management. It noted
that the law provides for an exception for the “local wisdom and traditional knowledge” of
swidden agriculture and added that Adat communities are expected to coordinate with the
relevant authorities when practicing swidden agriculture. In such instances, and as a risk
management measure, a fire truck may be positioned on scene. District authorities spoke
passionately about the importance of traditional knowledge and recognized the close bond that
Long Isun and other customary communities have with the forest. A senior district official
emphasized that Adat communities have practiced swidden agriculture for generations and their
forests are still there, noting that forest fires typically occur in the context of land clearing for
palm oil plantations.

68. The Panel saw the banners saying “Stop Forest and Land Fires – Guard and Love Our
Surrounding Environment” 65 at several locations in the forested areas of the province, including
around Long Isun. The Panel notes that the banners do not appear to target any specific
community. The community explained to the Panel team that members continue to farm and
access the forest despite the banners, although they are mindful of adhering to the law and
prevent forest fires. The Panel observes that the Request recognizes that these prohibitions
reflect a broader trend in national and regional policy frameworks and that no distinction is
made for customary, small-scale, and ecologically sustainable practices. 66

69. Alleged retaliation against the community. Although the Request raises instances of
retaliation, during the Panel’s visit community members reported no such instances. However,

E.3 The Panel’s Review

71. This section establishes:
 i) Whether there is a plausible, causal link between the alleged harm and the Project.
 ii) Whether the harm may be significant and the noncompliance of serious character.
 iii) Whether Management dealt appropriately with the issues raised in the Request and
 demonstrated clearly that it has followed or is taking steps to follow the required
 policies and procedures, or Management acknowledged that it did not comply with
 relevant policies and procedures.
 iv) Whether Management has provided a statement of specific remedial actions, and
 whether, in the judgment of the Panel and taking into account the view of the
 Requesters, these proposed remedial actions may adequately address the matters
 raised by the Request. 67

72. The Panel appreciates the extensive discussions it held with the Government of
Indonesia and the authorities of East Kalimantan Province and Mahakam Ulu District, and
recognizes the importance of this pilot Project in supporting the GoI’s Nationally Determined
Contribution to the Paris Agreement. The Panel acknowledges the serious concerns of the
Requesters and the community members with whom it spoke and appreciates the trust they
placed in the Panel’s process. It also appreciates the productive discussions it held with them
and the additional information shared during its visit. The Panel also acknowledges
Management’s detailed response to the issues raised in the Request. The remainder of this
section presents the Panel’s review of the allegations mentioned above; distinguishing between
those plausibly linked to the Project and those that are not plausibly linked to the Project. The
Panel considers the actions taken by the Project in response to the concerns first raised with the
GRS and subsequently with the Panel.

73. Allegations plausibly linked to the Project. Institutionalized discrimination and
exclusion caused by the implementation of the BSP. The Panel observes that that the original
BSP did not allow non-recognized Adat communities, including the Long Isun community, to
67 Inspection Panel Operating Procedures (2025), p. 15, para. 45.
 19
 benefit from the Advance Payment. It also notes that the original BSP did not provide equitable
benefit sharing because it focused on incentivizing reduced deforestation and forest
degradation and did not recognize the ecosystem services provided by communities, such as
Long Isun, that have continuously protected and preserved their forests. The Panel considers
that both these weaknesses may have constituted harm to the Long Isun community.

74. The Panel further observes that, following the Requesters’ complaints to the GRS,
Management recognized these weaknesses and potential non-compliances in the original BSP,
and the Project initiated a BSP revision, as well as additional consultations. First, this BSP
revision resulted in all customary communities, irrespective of whether they are MHA-
recognized, to benefit from the Reward Allocation. Second, the formula underpinning the
distribution of the Performance Allocation was revised to ensure more equitable benefit sharing
by better balancing incentives for villages to protect and preserve their forest and reward those
that, like Long Isun, have done this all along. Management also explained that the revised BSP
has removed all private sector roles.

75. The Panel also notes the Requesters’ claim that not withdrawing their forest from the
Project’s ER accounting constitutes serious harm. The Panel considers that the Project’s
jurisdictional approach, covering the entire province of East Kalimantan, does not constitute
material harm. It further considers that the alleged harm raised in the Request has been
addressed and that the Long Isun village and community retain the option to re-engage with
and opt into the Project’s benefit sharing.

76. The Panel notes the Bank’s commitment to continue monitoring implementation of the
revised BSP, even though the Project closed on December 31, 2025. The Panel understands
that the Government’s engagement with the beneficiary villages and communities in East
Kalimantan province will continue, as the Final Payment and any additional carbon credits the
Government receives will be shared in accordance with the revised BSP, and that the Bank will
continue to monitor its implementation.

77. Inadequate consultations. The Panel notes the Requesters’ allegation that consultations
early in the Project were not meaningful. It observes that Management and provincial
authorities acknowledged that initial consultations were insufficient and that communities were
inadequately informed about the Project and its objective. The Panel further notes that the
community lacked basic knowledge of Project operations, the revised BSP formula, the
conditions for accessing the shared benefits, and the Project’s impact (or lack thereof) on their
access to the forest and use of ancestral land.

78. The Panel observes that, after receiving the GRS complaints, the Project increased its
efforts to engage and consult with villages and community stakeholders, particularly during the
revision of the BSP and the socialization of the revised BSP and the Final Payment. The Panel
notes, however, that after opting out, the Long Isun community declined further contact with
Government staff involved in the ER Program, and the Project acknowledged and respected
this decision. The Panel also observes that the Project’s engagement efforts will involve further
consultations and information sessions, including with the Long Isun community, if it were to
reconsider and decide opting into the Project’s benefit sharing. The Panel considers that the
alleged weaknesses in consultations are being addressed.

79. Instances of retaliation. The Panel notes that the Request describes several instances of
retaliation and intimidation towards the Long Isun community. The Panel observes that after
 20
 the Project took the allegation of retaliation seriously, it raised these concerns with the
authorities at various levels. The community confirmed to the Panel that there have been no
new instances of retaliation since their complaint to the GRS. The Panel considers that the
community’s fear of retaliation in relation to the Project is being addressed.

80. Allegations not plausibly linked to the Project. Delayed recognition of Long Isun as
an Adat community. The Panel understands that the alleged delay in MHA recognition goes to
the heart of Long Isun community’s ability to protect its forest, which is a central concern of
this Request. The Panel observes that MHA recognition is supported by the Project through
Component 1 and that an administrative process is in place for applying for and being granted
MHA recognition. The Panel notes that any potential delay affecting the recognition process
may be rooted in, generally, multi-layered administrative and procedural requirements and the
limited financial and institutional capacity of district authorities, and, more specifically, the
boundary dispute of the Long Isun community with a neighboring community. The Panel
determines that such delays are not attributable to the Project. The Panel also notes that the
submission of the Request appears to have created a momentum that accelerated the recognition
process. The Panel has been informed that the MHA for the Long Isun community is awaiting
a final signature from the highest-level of the district authority. The Panel understands that, at
the time of the submission of its recommendation, this signature was still pending.

81. Disregard of the customary right to occupy, use, and manage ancestral lands. The Panel
recognizes that the Long Isun community’s rights to manage and protect their ancestral lands
are essential to the community’s identity and survival. Community members explained to the
Panel that they rely on the forest for food security, medicine, and resources for artisanal
products which sustain their culture and livelihoods. However, the Panel notes that the Project
does not affect the Long Isun community’s existing land and land-use rights, nor does it impose
new restrictions on access to or use of their ancestral lands, forest, or forest resources. The
Panel determines that these allegations are not linked to the Project.

82. Gender-based violence, exclusion, and discrimination against women. The Panel
recognizes the importance of forest resources and traditional farming to women’s livelihoods,
food security, and their cultural roles. It notes that the alleged restrictions on forest access are
unrelated to the Project, and that women of Long Isun confirmed they continue to farm and
access the forest as usual. The Panel also recognizes broader challenges faced by Adat women,
including discrimination and exclusion. However, the Panel observes that women did not report
any incidents of physical or sexual violence, nor any acts that could be considered as GBV.
Therefore, the Panel determines these allegations are not linked to the Project.

F. Recommendation

83. The Panel notes that the Requesters and the Request for Inspection meet all six technical
eligibility criteria set forth in the Panel Resolution in relation to the allegations pertaining to i)
institutionalized discrimination and exclusion resulting from the implementation of the original
BSP, ii) inadequate consultations, and iii) retaliation.

84. However, the Panel observes that Management acknowledged the weaknesses and
potential non-compliances related to these allegations. The Panel further notes that, as
described above, the Project has taken, and continues to take, steps to address these issues and
has therefore dealt with them appropriately. First, Management prompted the Project to revise
the BSP to allow for a more equitable distribution of funds under the Reward and Performance

 21
 Allocations, which will also benefit the Long Isun community should it decide to opt into the
ER Program’s benefit sharing. Second, following the BSP revision, the Project increased its
efforts to engage and consult with villages and community stakeholders. Third, Management
raised the community’s concerns about fear of retaliation with authorities at various levels, and
the community confirmed to the Panel that there have been no new instances of retaliation. The
Panel considers that these steps have addressed, or are in the process of addressing, the
allegations raised by the Requesters that are plausibly linked to the Project.

85. In the light of the above, the Panel does not recommend an investigation into the
allegations raised in the Request. The Panel notes that, since the Project was approved after
September 8, 2020, this recommendation does not preclude the possibility of a future Request
for Inspection based on new evidence or circumstances not known at the time of the current
Request. If the Board of Executive Directors concurs with this recommendation, the Panel will
advise the Requesters and Management accordingly.

  3. The Project

The project at issue is the East Kalimantan Project for ER Results (P166244),5 financed by the
World Bank through the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF) (hereafter ER Project). The
ER Project forms part of the broader REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest
Degradation) framework, a global initiative designed to create financial incentives for developing
countries to conserve forests and reduce carbon emissions.

In theory, REDD+ aims to mitigate climate change while providing benefits to forest-dependent
communities. In practice, however, many REDD+ projects worldwide have been criticized for
replicating top-down, market-based conservation models that exclude Indigenous Peoples,
undermine customary tenure, and commodity forest ecosystems. These projects often proceed
without resolving underlying tenure insecurity or recognizing Indigenous governance systems,
conditions that are essential for equitable climate action.6

In Indonesia, the ER Project operates within the national SIS-REDD+ (Safeguard Information
System for REDD+) framework,7 which the Government established to comply with UNFCCC
Cancun Safeguards and to ensure that REDD+ implementation "respects the rights of Indigenous
Peoples, promotes full and effective participation, protects natural forests, and enhances social
and environmental benefits." Under SIS-REDD+, implementing partners, including the World
Bank as the financier of the FCPF program, are obligated to:

 • Guarantee respect for Indigenous rights and customary tenure (aligned with Constitutional
 Court Decision No. 35/2012)
 • Ensure free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) before any activity affecting Indigenous
 territories
 • Prevent displacement or restriction of customary practices
 • Facilitate benefit-sharing that is transparent, equitable, and inclusive of all affected
 Indigenous groups.8

The ER Project in East Kalimantan reflects these systemic issues, and fails to meet the
aforementioned safeguards. It was intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from

process has been frozen, as formal recognition of Long lsun as MHA is a legal prerequisite.42 The
ESIA itself acknowledged that revocation of permits and status quo designations create risks of
unmanaged lands, deforestation, and heightened tensions.43 It also emphasized that recognition
of customary lands was urgent for inclusion of Indigenous Peoples.44

Despite this, the Bank allowed Long lsun's disputed lands to be included in ER Project benefit
calculations, without recognition, without dispute resolution, and without consent. This violates
the FPIC principles in OP 4.10, paras. 10-11. The Bank should have supported a forest
management that protects the rights and participation of forest-dependent Indigenous Peoples as
required under OP 4.36, paras, 1-3, but failed to do so.

 c. Recognition of MHA: A Structural Barrier Ignored


41
 Although para. 8 formally applies to Category A projects, its underlying principle, that affected communities
must have the genuine ability to reject or propose alternatives to harmful projects, remains fundamental to the
Bank's due diligence obligations, especially where Category B projects carry substantial social risks and affect
Indigenous Peoples' rights to FPIC.
42
 The Ministry of Environment and Forestry of Indonesia, Ministerial Regulation no. 9/2021, article 66(2) stipulates
that any request for a Customary Forest declaration requires MHA status.

 Recognition as MHA is the legal foundation for Indigenous Peoples in Indonesia to secure tenure,
protect forests, and access benefit-sharing. Yet in East Kalimantan, only four Indigenous groups
have been recognized as MHA, and none of the 50 villages in Mahakam Ulu, including Long lsun,
have been recognized.45 This leaves an entire district excluded from MHA protections. The SESA
acknowledged this problem,46 and the ER Project formally committed to support provincial
government efforts to accelerate recognition of customary rights.47 In practice, however, the Bank
disclaimed responsibility, arguing that recognition falls outside the Project's scope. This is a
fundamental abdication of safeguard obligations.

 • Since Indigenous Peoples are present in, and collectively. attached to, the Long lsun
 territory, the borrower and implementing agency was required to carry out a social
 assessment to evaluate the project's potential adverse impacts and examine project
 alternatives. This was not done in a meaningful or adequate way. The assessment did not
 account for Long lsun's unresolved land boundary conflict with - and -·
 nor the exclusionary effects of delayed MHA recognition. Without such an assessment,
 the Project failed to consider alternatives that could have avoided or mitigated these

 • OP 4.10 para. 17 requires that when projects depend on establishing legally recognized

 was prepared for Long lsun, even after a complaint was formally filed with the GRS and

 • OP 4.10 para. 22(a) directs the Bank to support legal reforms, capacity building, and

 Indigenous Peoples benefit from development. The ER Project failed to do so.

The Project Appraisal Document itself acknowledged the risk: "The risk of exclusion of Indigenous
groups stemming from the slow recognition process."" The Bank thus proceeded in full
knowledge of the risks, but without implementing any safeguard actions to prevent exclusion or

commercialized, performance-based mechanism dominated by corporate and state actors.

 • Intimidation of allied organizations (PNP), with insinuations that pursuing the complaint

These reprisals had a chilling effect: Long lsun representatives felt forced to attend consultations
against their will, while refusing to sign attendance sheets to avoid misrepresentation. The fear of

The World Bank has clear obligations under OP 4.10 para. 10(c), which requires that all relevant
information about the project be provided in a culturally appropriate manner at each stage of
project preparation and implementation, and that such consultations are conducted in good faith
and in a manner that is free of intimidation or coercion. This includes informing communities not

In practice, Long lsun was subjected to repeated threats: warnings that village development funds
would be cut off if they refused to attend consultations; pressure from ER Project representatives
threatening to escalate matters to district authorities if the community did not participate; and
suggestions that pursuing a complaint would antagonize all districts and jeopardize provincial
funding. These are not abstract risks but concrete reprisals designed to coerce Long lsun into
compliance.

The Bank also maintains a zero-tolerance policy on reprisals and requires that grievance redress
mechanisms be accessible, safe, and free from retaliation. Yet, despite being notified of these
threats in writing, including through formal correspondence to the GRS, the Bank failed to take
protective measures. No safeguards were activated to shield Long lsun or their allies from
intimidation, and no monitoring was established to ensure their safety when engaging with Bank

By ignoring retaliation and intimidation, the Bank violated OP 4.10 para. 10(c), undermined its
own safeguards, and denied Long lsun safe access to accountability mechanisms. This failure
erodes the credibility of both the GRS and the Bank's broader commitments to protect Indigenous
Peoples who exercise their right to reject harmful projects.

6. Ignoring Livelihood Impacts and Customary Practices (in violation of OP4.10: 16)

The livelihoods of Long lsun are deeply tied to customary practices such as small-scale logging,
swidden farming (/adang berpindah), controlled burning, hunting, and forest gathering. These
customary practices are sustainable, culturally embedded, and central to food security, health,
and income. Women, in particular, play key roles by gathering plants for food, medicine, and
handicrafts such as the Seraung hat. Long lsun women have also established a women farmer
group who engage in swidden farming.

The SESA itself acknowledged that REDD+ activities could restrict these practices, particularly
burning, and that such restrictions could negatively impact Indigenous livelihoods and cultural
traditions. Despite this, no mitigation measures or livelihood alternatives were developed or
implemented. Instead, after ER Project socializations, local authorities began issuing prohibitions


 26
 on burning, disrupting traditional farming cycles and threatening subsistence food production. For
Long lsun, this created fear of criminalization, recalling their past experiences of being targeted
during land disputes with -· The Project thereby contributed to a climate of insecurity in
which communities risk losing not only their livelihoods but also their dignity and safety. This
omission violates multiple safeguard obligations:

 • OP 4.01 para. 3 requires the Bank to ensure environmental and social assessment
 identifies and mitigates adverse impacts on Indigenous Peoples and it includes the social
 aspects such as their livelihoods. The Bank's failure to assess or mitigate livelihood
 disruptions shows noncompliance with this foundational requirement.
 • OP 4.10 para. 16 explicitly recognizes that Indigenous Peoples are "closely tied to land,
 forests, water, wildlife, and other natural resources," and that special considerations apply
 when projects affect such ties. In such cases, the borrower must pay attention to (a)
 customary rights to lands and resources; (b) the need to protect such lands against
 intrusion or encroachment; (c) the cultural and spiritual values attached to those
 resources; and (d) Indigenous natural resource management practices and their
 sustainability. The ER Project failed to uphold these requirements. Instead of protecting
 Long lsun's customary rights and practices, it facilitated restrictions and created conditions
 of insecurity.
 • OP 4.12 para. 3(b) requires the Bank to avoid or minimize involuntary restrictions of
 access to resources, and where such restrictions are unavoidable, to provide sustainable
 livelihood restoration measures. The ER Project potentially imposes de facto access
 restrictions through burning prohibitions and forest-use limits, without consultation,
 consent, or compensatory alternatives.
 • OP 4.36 paras. 1-3 emphasize that forest sector interventions must recognize the rights
 and participation of forest-dependent communities, and support sustainable local resource
 management rather than constrain it. The ER Project disregarded these obligations by
 incentivizing criminalization of traditional forest use instead of reinforcing community
 stewardship.

By failing to safeguard livelihoods, the Bank not only violated its policies but also placed Long
lsun at risk of poverty, food insecurity, and dependency on government or concessionaire-
controlled programs. This is directly contrary to the stated objectives of REDD+ to improve
wellbeing and reduce poverty.
