  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


The Project
i. The East Kalimantan Project for Emission Reductions Results (P166244, the “Project”)
 aimed to provide payment from the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility Carbon Fund
 (FCPF-CF) for verified emission reductions (ER) from Reduced Deforestation and Forest
 Degradation (REDD+) across the province of East Kalimantan in Indonesia. The Project
 served as a financing vehicle for the ER generated under the Government’s East
 Kalimantan Jurisdictional Emission Reductions Program (ER Program), which is
 financed and implemented by the Government of Indonesia and described in an Emission
 Reductions Program Document (ERPD). The Project was approved by the Regional Vice
 President (RVP) on November 24, 2020, and closed on December 31, 2025.

ii. The ERPD sets out the ER Program implemented at the scale of East Kalimantan Province,
 covering approximately 12.7 million hectares (ha) of land and 6.5 million ha of forest
 across seven districts and three cities. The ER Program aims to reduce emissions while
 supporting improved land governance, sustainable development, and livelihoods for
 Indigenous Peoples and local communities, and is embedded within Indonesia’s national
 REDD+ framework and climate commitments. The Project was governed by two legal
 agreements, known as the Emission Reduction Purchase Agreements (ERPA), 1 between
 the Republic of Indonesia, represented by the Ministry of Environment and Forestry
 (MoEF) 2 (the “Government”) and the World Bank (the “Bank”) acting as Trustee of the
 FCPF (see paragraphs 5–30 for more details).

iii. The Project Development Objective was to incentivize reduced deforestation and forest
 degradation in East Kalimantan, through payment of verified ER, and to help ensure that
 paid amounts were distributed according to an agreed Benefit Sharing Plan (BSP).

iv. Based on the jurisdictional nature of the ER Program, a systems approach was applied for
 the implementation of environmental and social safeguards applicable to both the
 Government’s ER Program and the BSP. This systems approach—which is akin to the
 Bank’s approach for financial intermediary operations—does not involve Bank supervision
 of the individual activities under the ER Program. Environmental and social (E&S) risks
 were managed through the Government’s Environmental and Social Management System
 (ESMS), complemented by Project-specific instruments. The Bank monitored E&S
 performance at an aggregated systems level, based on confirmation of the ability of the
 Government ESMS to manage the E&S risks and impacts of those individual activities (see
 paragraphs 16, 31–38 for more details).




1
  Two ERPA were signed for this operation on November 25, 2020—one for Tranche A of the Carbon Fund, and one
for Tranche B. Both are referred to when the ERPA is referenced in the context of this operation and the Request.
2
  Following an 2024 institutional reorganization in Indonesia, ERPA responsibilities were split between the Ministry
of Forestry, which is the technical lead on forest governance, management and REDD+, and the Ministry of
Environment, which is responsible for carbon transactions and results-based payments under the ERPA.


 vi

 v. The Government’s ESMS was assessed and gap-filling measures were identified where
 needed. Supervision focused on reviews of the periodic environmental and social system-
 level performance reporting by the Government. Some reporting gaps occurred, and the
 sequencing and arrangements were clarified and consolidated during implementation (see
 paragraphs 39–45).


The Request

vi. On December 23, 2025, the Inspection Panel registered a Request for Inspection, IPN
 Request RQ25/07 (hereafter referred to as the “Request”), concerning the Project. The
 Request for Inspection was submitted by members of the Dayak Bahau customary

xiv. The legal MHA recognition process is a multi-step, regionally led, and highly complex

 III. BACKGROUND ON THE ER PROGRAM AND THE PROJECT

5. The East Kalimantan Project for Emission Reductions Results (the Project) aimed to
provide payment from the FCPF-CF for verified emission reductions (ER) from Reduced
Deforestation and Forest Degradation (REDD+) across the province of East Kalimantan in
Indonesia. The Project served as a financing vehicle for the ER generated under the East
Kalimantan Jurisdictional Emission Reductions Program (“ER Program”), which is financed and
implemented by the Government of Indonesia and described in an Emission Reduction Program
Document (ERPD). The Project focused on providing results-based payments for achieved ER
rather than on financing the ER Program activities themselves. In the jurisdictional REDD+
approach, ER are measured against a historic reference level. This reference level is an agreed
aggregate average of past deforestation and associated CO2 equivalent emissions across a large
territory, such as a country or province, representing what would have occurred in the absence of
the ER Program.

6. The FCPF provided the funding to pay for the ER generated. The FCPF is a global
partnership launched in 2008 to support developing countries in implementing REDD+ activities.
The FCPF mobilized over US$1.3 billion from 17 donors 3 to support this global partnership, which
is implemented through two multi-donor trust funds for which the Bank acts as a Trustee and fund
manager: (i) the Readiness Fund (now closed), and (ii) the Carbon Fund (operational through
2028), which provided the payments for the ER achieved by the East Kalimantan ER Program.

7. ER programs are designed and implemented by governments. The Bank conducts the
necessary due diligence of country reports, including the commissioning of independent
verification of ER and review of country environmental and social (E&S) systems. To inform the
independent verification of ER, countries submit an Emission Reductions Monitoring Report
(ERMR) to the FCPF-CF to demonstrate and claim verified ER from ER Program measures over
a specific reporting period. 4 The Bank, however, does not have a specific operation financing the
underlying ER Program measures set out in a government’s ER program. On behalf of the FCPF,
the Bank only makes results-based payments for achieved and verified ER.


Government Jurisdictional Programs for Emission Reductions under the FCPF

ER across a large-scale, administratively defined jurisdiction (e.g., province, state, or nation).
Government ER Program measures are financed by the respective governments or by other
entities, including in some cases by the Bank, but then through an operation separate from the
FCPF payment for the ER. In the case of this Project, no parallel Bank operation is providing
financing for the Government ER Program measures. The results-based payment for a
government’s ER program is approved by the FCPF Carbon Fund Participants Committee, 5 which

 IV. SAFEGUARDS APPROACH TO THE PROJECT


Applicable Bank Policy Framework

31. The Bank Directive on Managing Environmental and Social Risks and Impacts for the
Emission Reductions Programs under the Forest Carbon Partnership Facility and the
BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes (the Directive), 22 and the legal
agreement (the ERPA) between the Bank and the Government for the particular operation, together
set out the respective obligations of the Bank and the Government to comply with the Bank’s E&S
policies with regard to: (i) the implementation of ER Program measures; and (ii) the plan according
to which the financial benefits generated from ER are distributed to government entities and others,
including local communities (the BSP).

32. As explained below, the Bank applies a systems approach to supervise the management
of E&S risks. This approach is commensurate with the jurisdictional nature of ER Programs, under
which results-based payments are made for verified ER generated through a wide range of
government-financed investments, activities, and policy actions at the national and subnational
levels.

33. Under this arrangement, the Project focused on providing results-based payments for
achieved ER rather than on financing the ER Program activities themselves. Its role, as the
FCPF Trustee, is to make payments for verified ER to the Government entity in charge of the ER
Program. E&S risks are managed through the Government’s ESMS, complemented by project-
specific instruments. This systems approach—which is akin to the Bank’s approach for financial
intermediary operations under OP 4.01—does not involve Bank supervision of the individual
activities under the ER Program. Rather, the Bank monitors E&S performance at an aggregated
systems level, based on confirmation of the ability of the Government ESMS to manage the E&S
risks and impacts of those individual activities.

34. During the Project preparation phase, the Directive requires that ER Program measures and
benefit-sharing arrangements (BSP) be defined, and that E&S risks and impacts be identified and
assessed through a SESA prepared by the Government. The Bank assesses the Government’s
ESMS against the Bank’s E&S policies, and any identified gaps must be addressed through
measures incorporated into relevant E&S framework instruments (e.g., the ESMF and the IPPF).

35. During the implementation phase, the Directive requires the Bank to monitor and support
the Government’s implementation of its ESMS, safeguard instruments, and BSP. Bank supervision
focuses on periodic reviews of system-level performance and self-reporting. The Bank does not
review or clear individual E&S assessments or plans, nor does it provide implementation support
for individual ER Program measures or BSP activities. Rather, it conducts implementation support
missions and reviews of the Government’s ERMRs, which are submitted at the end of each
reporting period, and regular E&S Management Reports after each reporting period. The Directive
also requires third-party monitoring (TPM) of the implementation of the ESMS, BSP, and

drivers of deforestation, and conducted extensive consultations with Indigenous Peoples, local
communities, civil society, and government institutions.

37. Building on this work, the Government conducted an ESDD assessment in 2020 to
evaluate the adequacy of existing systems for managing E&S risks under the ER Program. The
ESDD audited the ESMS, which was a precondition for payment of ER generated during the first
reporting period (June 2019–November 2020). The audit focused on system capacity related to
E&S risk management for the ER Program measures implemented during that period. Government
implementing agencies participated in data collection and verification through electronic surveys
and in-depth interviews.

manage the E&S risks associated with the ER Program in a manner consistent with the Bank’s
safeguard policies. The Bank accepted the ESDD in November 2021.

the Government to monitor and report annually on the implementation of E&S management

reviewed by the Bank in accordance with the ESMF and complemented by TPM, as required.

46. The Requesters’ claims, accompanied by Management’s detailed responses, are provided

47. Management has carefully reviewed the Long Isun community’s concerns and
concludes that they largely fall outside the remit of the Project and the Bank. Those that relate
to the Project have been appropriately addressed. For the most part, the Requesters raise issues
similar to those raised with the Bank in March 2024 through a complaint to the Grievance
Redress Service (GRS). Since that complaint, the Bank has engaged intensively with the
Requesters and their representatives, including through a Bank mission to Long Isun’s territory, to
address the Project-related concerns. However, their main concerns cannot be addressed by the
Project and the Bank because they are unrelated to the Project, predate it, or are not governed by
Bank policy.

48. At the heart of the Request lies Long Isun’s demand for legal recognition as an
indigenous (“adat”) group in Indonesia. Management appreciates the importance of this
recognition for the Requesters, but highlights that it follows an application process under
Indonesian law, known as “Masyarakat Hukum Adat (MHA) legal recognition,” that is a
sovereign matter for the Government of Indonesia, and not within the remit of the Bank or the
Project. The Long Isun community’s application for legal MHA recognition dates back to 2018—
before the ER Program and the Project—and delays in the process cannot be attributed to the
Project.

49. On the contrary, the ER Program supported the Requesters’ application by: (i) setting
up district-level MHA verification committees to facilitate the recognition process; and (ii)
providing resources to the provincial and district Community Empowerment and Village
Government Agency (DPMPD) to support local communities in the application process. Legal
MHA recognition could not be guaranteed by the Project, and was not a precondition to Project
activities, or a requirement of Bank policy. Moreover, the local government’s recent announcement
of the conclusion of the verification for Long Isun’s application for legal MHA recognition
indicates that the ER Program has not jeopardized or undermined Long Isun’s ability to obtain
such recognition.

50. Management further notes that the Request’s claims of adverse impacts on the Long
Isun community stemming from the Project are not substantiated, given that no ER Program
measures that could lead to land use restrictions took place in Long Isun during the ERPA
reporting periods (2019–2024) (see paragraph 16, above). 23 The only ER Program measures that
were reported by the Government to have been implemented in Long Isun were: (i) the provision
of technical assistance by the local government to support Long Isun’s legal MHA recognition
claim; and (ii) the establishment of an MPA. Both activities are voluntary in nature and were
specifically requested and supported by the Long Isun community. The Requesters expressed
concern about restrictions on the use of traditional forest fires and cultivation practices. But the

Delayed Legal MHA Recognition

54. In Indonesia, the formal recognition process for MHA—i.e., indigenous, or customary
law/adat communities—is multi-step, regionally led, and a complex process under current laws
and policies. Recognition gives a community legal status as a distinct adat community and is a
prerequisite for securing rights over land or forests claimed as traditional territory. The Request
alleges that the delayed formal recognition of Long Isun’s indigenous status by the Government
was an “outcome of the project design.”

55. The Dayak Bahau customary community of Long Isun has long sought formal

strengthen participation and outreach on ER Program and BSP implementation, including by
training field facilitators that speak local languages. This included meaningful consultations with
the Long Isun community in 2024, at which point the Long Isun community decided to opt out of
the ER Program. From then on, the Requesters asked that they no longer be contacted by
Government staff in relation to the ER Program. This request was acknowledged and respected.
Should Long Isun wish to re-engage in the ER Program and receive funds through the BSP from
the final ERPA payment, the revised 2025 BSP now includes requirements for improved
consultations approaches and stronger guidance on conducting consultation with Indigenous
Peoples.

the Government would not first grant them legal MHA recognition or agree to their demand to
exclude Long Isun from the Program’s accounting area. However, these two demands from the
community, which are discussed in paragraphs 55 and 61, do not indicate that the consultations
were not meaningful.

104. Management acknowledges certain weaknesses in supervision and follow-up on the
Government’s ESMS reporting during the first phase of Project implementation. In addition, there
were delays and weaknesses with regard to consultations during the COVID-19 restrictions on
travel and gatherings. However, these issues were identified and corrected during implementation.
In Management’s view, these challenges have had little or no relevance for the issues raised by the
Long Isun adat community, especially considering its decision to eventually opt out and not
participate in further consultations or the BSP.

105. Management concludes that the Bank has correctly applied its policies and procedures in
relation to the matters raised in the Request. Accordingly, in Management’s view the Requesters’

 — Summary of adjustments to the Benefit Sharing Plan and Indigenous Peoples Plan —


A series of public consultations was undertaken on the revision of the Benefit Sharing Plan (BSP) and draft
Indigenous Peoples Plan (IPP) for the ER Program. The public consultation involved outreach and actions
to gather broad-based input from communities and their representatives in East Kalimantan, as well as from
Government representatives.
Design of and implementation of consultations:
The public consultation process was designed based on substantive inputs, both from formal and informal
means, from a range of actors in East Kalimantan. Specifically, civil society organizations were asked to
advise on the structure and format of the consultation process, and how the process might effectively and
efficiently solicit broad-based and meaningful input from groups likely to be affected by the Benefit Sharing
Plan, especially adat communities.
Formal ‘pre-consultations’ were hosted in partnership with universities and CSO on behalf of the
Government. This has been done through soliciting direct input from civil society since 16 July 2025, and
through roundtable discussions with these civil society representatives and leaders. In addition, Faculty of
Forestry of the University of Mulawarman independently hosted an event on July 28th, 2025, which aimed
to support preparation for the public consultation process and provide stakeholders a voice in both how the
consultations would be managed, and support preparation for stakeholders who wished to engage. Over 20
local CSOs attended the event, which gathered inputs on the publicly disclosed documents. University
members and The Regional Climate Change Council (DDPI) co-moderated the session, which discussed
BSP implementation, such as how adat communities can access and use carbon payments, eligibility
criteria, and community outreach and safeguards processes. The meeting concluded with a mapping of key
concerns of the local CSOs and academia representatives, which were then conveyed to the Government
during the public consultation process.
These events solicited the following input, which then informed the design of the government-led
consultation process:

 • In-person consultations should extend at least to the district level and should invite a broad range
 of community-level representatives.

 • Civil society groups from across the province should be not only invited, but meaningfully
 included as moderators and speakers, to create an open forum for discussion.

 • Adat leaders – particularly those who are not sitting in the formally recognized Government
 positions (e.g., those who are not elected Village Heads) should be invited.

 • Communications and outreach materials should be made widely available to explain the BSP and
 IPP. They should be in clear and accessible language and easy to understand and disseminated
 widely to support meaningful engagement of community-level participants, either online, in
 person, via representatives from their villages or districts who attend in-person meetings or make
 submissions.

Consultation outcomes:
This document presents a summary of the inputs received on the BSP and IPP combined through both online
feedback forums and in-person events, and how it has been incorporated into an updated benefits sharing
plan. The summary of issues below reflects all issues that were raised by three or more participants /
feedback providers.
Topic 1: The size of allocations for community groups through the reward allocation. Several
participants queried why the reward allocation overall and the grants sizes for eligible recipients were not
higher.




 Official Use Only
  East Kalimantan Project for Emission Reductions Results


 Response: Community groups and members can participate in both responsibility allocations (which
  funds government-delivered programs, some of which are aimed at local communities, such as
  accelerating MHA recognition), and performance allocations (which are administered via Village
  Governments, following community-led planning processes of which all local residents are free to
  participate in). Therefore, the reward allocation is an additional entitlement specifically for community
  groups with a historical relationship to conserved forest areas (from which the ER payment was most
  likely not generating, as it measures reductions in deforestation). Moreover, the reward allocation gives
  grants significantly larger than all other carbon finance projects which have provided community grants
  to date (e.g. the Nusantara Fund).
Action taken: The costs of community facilitation and support from the LEMTARA have been allocated
from the responsibility allocation, to ensure the full 10% of the reward allocation for community groups
goes to the groups.
Topic 2: The involvement of local partners. Participants highlighted the importance of local NGOs and
adat organizations playing a role in community support and outreach.
 Response: The role for local NGOs and CSOs is recognized, and will be accommodated to the extent
  possible within the regulatory framework which governs funds channeling through the BPDLH.
  Specifically, agencies contracted by BPDLH are required to comply with Director of BPDLH
  Regulation Number 3 of 2024, and must also be able to submit financial and activity reports sufficient
  to fulfil the requirements of the audit BPDLH will be subject to on use of funds.
 Action taken: The revised BSP expands the number of LEMTARA that will be contracted by BPDLH
  to support local communities from one national agency to four subnational agencies, with a dedicated
  agency focused on Masyarakat Adat. These four agencies will engage local CSOs to deliver community
  related activities.
Topic 3: Surplus budget utilization (SiLPA). Several participants highlighted the challenge that budgets
not utilized within a fiscal year may present challenges in the absence of clarity on whether they can be
carried over, and/or whether they contribute to village government spending performance ratings. This is a
particular challenge if funds are delivered late in the fiscal year, leaving a limited spending window.
 Response: The unused budget (SiLPA) can be used in the following year based on prevailing laws and
  regulations.
 Actions taken: The BSP is updated to clarify how SiLPA funds are classified and utilized, and with
 stronger guidance on aligning with budgeting cycles, to avoid late delivery of funds.
Topic 4: Inclusion of women’s groups and persons with disabilities (PWD). Participants suggested that
community groups representing women and PWD should be including as ‘community groups’ eligible for
the reward allocation.
 Response: Expanding eligibility for the reward allocation will further squeeze limited use of funds
  intended to recognize historical forest protection and provide support to adat communities.
 Action taken: Annex 3 of the BSP has been updated to clarify that funds allocated to villages and
  communities can be allocated to support social or economic groups or initiatives within their

 ANNEX 4. LEGAL MHA RECOGNITION PROCESS OVERVIEW



The legal MHA recognition process involves the following steps:

 • Community Self-Identification and Preparation. Adat communities and their traditional
 institutions (adat leadership, customary councils) must prepare documentation proving
 that they meet criteria such as: (i) customary institutional structure (adat governance); (ii)
 continued observance of customary/adat norms; (iii) clear territorial boundaries; and (iv)
 historical continuity of the community’s existence and customary/adat practices.

 • Submission of Recognition Request: The community then formally applies for recognition
 by submitting its documentation to the subnational government (usually at the district or
 provincial level). The community itself acts as the petitioner.

 • Sub-National Government Review and Validation: The subnational government reviews
 the application through MHA verification committees. This often involves: assessing the
 documentation, verifying traditional territorial boundaries, consulting relevant adat
 leaders, and potentially conducting local field verification. Sub-national governments act
 as facilitators and validators at this stage.

 • Legal Recognition by Local Government Decree: If the verification process is concluded
 by the MHA verification committee, the local authority issues a formal legal decision
 recognizing the community as an MHA. Recognition can take several legal forms,
 including: district or provincial decrees covering one or more communities; a decree
 specific to a particular community; a regional administrative decree; or, in some cases,
 court decisions.

 • Post-Recognition Rights and Follow-Up. Once legally recognized as an MHA, the
 community can seek recognition of customary land and forests (e.g., Hutan Adat) through
 national ministries. To obtain Hutan Adat/ Customary Forest titling, additional procedures
 under the Ministry of Forestry apply, including ministerial regulation procedures to change
 land status from state forest to customary forest. Recognition as MHA strengthens the
 community’s standing in negotiations over land use and resource management with
 businesses and government agencies.

abstract: On November 3, 2025, the Inspection Panel received a Request for Inspection related to the World Bank–financed Indonesia: East Kalimantan Project for Emission Reductions Results, submitted by a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Perkumpulan Nurani Perempuan (PNP), representing members of the Long Isun community in East Kalimantan, with Accountability Counsel and the Forest Peoples Programme acting as international NGO advisors; the Requesters asked that their names remain confidential due to fear of retaliation, and on December 23, 2025, the Inspection Panel registered the Request . The Request alleges that the Project designed to incentivize reduced deforestation and forest degradation through payments for verified emission reductions and their distribution under an agreed Benefit Sharing Plan (BSP) is causing environmental and social harm by failing to recognize community land rights and customary land use, restricting cultural practices such as forest rituals and rotational swidden farming, and creating livelihood losses. The Panel found that the Requesters and the Request met all six technical eligibility criteria under the Panel Resolution for allegations related to institutionalized discrimination and exclusion from the original BSP, inadequate consultations, and retaliation, but also noted that Management acknowledged related weaknesses and potential non-compliances and that the Project had taken and continues to take appropriate corrective actions, including revising the BSP to enable a more equitable distribution of funds under the Reward and Performance Allocations, increasing engagement and consultations with villages and community stakeholders, and raising concerns about fear of retaliation with authorities, with the community confirming that no new instances of retaliation had occurred. In light of these actions, the Panel does not recommend an investigation into the allegations, noting that since the Project was approved after September 8, 2020, this recommendation does not preclude a future Request for Inspection based on new evidence or circumstances not known at the time, and if the Board of Executive Directors concurs, the Panel will advise the Requesters and Management accordingly.
